messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The abduction had lasted seventy-two hours in a windowless basement where the air grew thick with mildew and a guard’s heavy boots echoed against concrete. Malik, then seventeen, had learned to hold his breath when the metal door creaked open, memorizing the rhythmic clatter of chains and the low commands that filled the dark. He had come to believe that survival depended on staying utterly invisible, a lesson that stuck long after the rescue team cut the lock. Now, at nineteen, he carried that hyper-vigilance into his role as a detective. Yet when the sun dipped below the horizon, the memory of that swallowed daylight returned with a violence that left him gasping on his couch. Those memories refused to cooperate with his mind. He knew exactly what had happened, yet when he tried to speak about it to his girlfriend, the words dissolved, leaving only a hollow ache in his throat. Instead of pictures, he would hear the guard’s muttered threats and the metallic scrape of the lock, sudden enough to make him drop his coffee mug. Other times, the past arrived carrying the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image at all; a wave of panic would crash over him during patrol, his heart hammering as if the walls were closing in once more. Because these intrusive recurrences struck without warning and carried such raw intensity, he had developed a rigid habit of trying hard not to think about the trauma, forcing himself into avoidance to keep the floodgates shut. He started avoiding going out at night, telling his squad he had early dates when the heavy click of his patrol car door locking each evening became a trigger that instantly pulled him back to the basement. At the precinct, he began avoiding being touched; a colleague’s hand on his shoulder to hand him a file sent a jolt of dread through him, and he stepped back, claiming a sudden sensitivity to the station’s wool uniforms. Over the following weeks and months, the pattern repeated itself. Every time a memory breached his conscious mind, he reached immediately for suppression, spending his shifts standing near the perimeter of the evidence room, keeping his gloves on and his elbows tucked. The more he worked to block the intrusions, the more frequently his mind breached the walls he built, pulling him further into the dark and away from contact. His detective work was complicated by his inability to handle the evidence bags that required direct gloved contact, and he could not sit close to his girlfriend during quiet evenings when her legs naturally brushed his. He had come to believe that letting his guard down meant being trapped again, so he maintained a rigid distance that left his partner wondering where the man she met had gone. Now, after three years of sleepless nights and mounting suspicion from his supervisor, Malik sat in the intake office, fingers knotted around his jacket hem. He was ready to finally speak, though he was terrified the words would never come, hoping instead that someone could help him untangle the past from the present without losing his mind in the process.
